items.title: An action-packed Apple Pay ad has dropped & it is directed by Edgar Wright
items.content_html:
Edgar Wright is known for directing films like "Baby Driver" and "Shaun of the Dead" with his signature fast cuts and rhythmic action. His latest gig showcases the power of Apple Pay when a hero defeats his enemies thanks to the speed and security of his payment method.

It's a playful ad that does a great job of showcasing the feature, though credit to the teller having those purchases rung up mid-combat sequence.

items.title: Turkey to get Apple's first manufacturing academy outside US
items.content_html:
Free coding courses and advanced manufacturing training are coming to Turkey as Apple expands its education programs for students and businesses.

Apple will open seven training and developer facilities in Turkey, expanding its support for app development and advanced manufacturing. The investment includes five Apple Developer Academies, a Developer Center in Istanbul, and an Advanced Manufacturing Center (AMC) in Ankara.

Apple will open the five developer academies over the next three years, with the first launching in Istanbul in 2027. Each will offer a free, nine-month program covering coding, design, marketing, project management, and artificial intelligence.

The curriculum will also address accessibility, privacy, and sustainability as students learn app development and entrepreneurship skills. The expansion will add to Apple's existing network of 19 developer academies worldwide.

Of the project, Apple Chairman and former CEO Tim Cook said the company is proud to support a new generation of entrepreneurs in the coming years.

Apple's other Advanced Manufacturing Center is located in Houston, Texas | Image credit: Apple

Istanbul's Developer Center will open in 2027, giving developers and startups access to Apple experts, tools, and technical resources. Workshops, individual appointments, and events will cover app design, quality, and performance across Apple's platforms.

The Ankara AMC will open in 2028, becoming Apple's second such facility and the first outside the United States. Free training and consulting will cover AI, machine learning, predictive maintenance, automation, and robotics for small and medium-sized businesses.

Apple's first AMC opened in Houston, Texas in August. The company invested hundreds of millions of dollars into the project, which it hopes will bolster American manufacturing.

items.title: Incremental iOS 27.2.1, iPadOS, macOS updates arrive with bug fixes
items.content_html:
Apple has issued updates for iOS 27.2.1, iPadOS 27.2.1, and macOS 27.2.1, with the incremental update bringing a collection of bug fixes and performance improvements to users.

Apple released its 27.2 operating system updates on October 26 and is currently running a developer beta for the 27.3 updates. That hasn't stopped it from issuing a small update for the current version.

The updates are small, as the point release number .1 indicates, so you typically shouldn't expect feature updates at all. They are more updates that have bug fixes, security updates, and performance improvements, which you really should update your device to as soon as possible.

Slightly differing from previous incremental updates, users may see different build numbers for their products as opposed to the mainline release. Apple has created versions specific to some products, such as the iPhone Duo and the PROLED MacBook Pro.

The full list of updates are:

  • iOS 27.2.1 (Build number 24B8156)
  • iOS 27.2.1 (24B91034) for iPhone Duo
  • iPadOS 27.2.1 (24B8156)
  • macOS 27.2.1 (26B131)
  • macOS 27.2.1 (26B7131) for M6 MacBook Pro and iMac
  • macOS 27.2.1 (26B8132) for PROLED MacBook Pro
  • visionOS 27.2.1 (24N124)
  • watchOS 27.2.1 (24S132)

Apple also issued updates for earlier operating system generations:

  • iOS 26.7.3 (23H131)
  • iOS 18.7.12 (22H390)
  • iPadOS 26.7.3 (23H131)
  • iPadOS 18.7.12 (22H390)
  • macOS 26.7.3 (25G342)
  • macOS 15.8.3 (24H241)
  • watchOS 26.6.1 (23U95)

How to install iOS 27.2.1 on an iPhone

To manually install iOS 27.2.1 on an iPhone, open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update. Tap the iOS 27.2.1 update and follow the instructions.

If you have automatic updates enabled, this will be performed on your behalf.

items.title: Apple Intelligence gets registered for iPad, Mac use in China
items.content_html:
Apple Intelligence won't just be available on the iPhone in China, as Apple has registered with regulators to bring it to iPad and Mac as well.

After a two-year wait behind the rest of the world, the iOS 27.3 developer beta brought Apple Intelligence to China. However, while the initial introduction is on the iPhone, it won't be that way for very long.

According to the Chinese cyberspace regulator speaking to Reuters on November 9, Apple has registered for Apple Intelligence to be used on tablets and notebooks. That means it will be usable on Mac desktops, MacBooks, and iPads in the future.

This isn't Apple's only registration for Apple Intelligence in China. Back in July, it did the same thing but for iPhone and it got approved.

Evidently, the registration was limited to smartphones at the time, and a second set was required for other products.

While the news is good for Apple users in China, it's not a done deal yet. Registration with a regulator is not the same as being approved by the same entity, so there's a small chance it can go wrong.

China has many requirements when it comes to tech, including regulatory approval for many different services, like generative AI. When it comes to U.S. companies, they usually have to work with a local partner to gain the necessary approval.

In the case of Apple Intelligence, Apple has worked with Alibaba to train a China-specific large language model. During the iPhone announcement for Apple Intelligence, Apple said it is still working with Alibaba to add Qianwen support within Siri.

A slow start in China

The initial wave of Apple Intelligence features arriving in China won't be the current Western experience of the AI toolset at first. Instead, it will look a lot like Apple Intelligence's early existence.

That means features like Photos Clean Up to tidy images, memory videos, and natural language search. Visual Intelligence using the iPhone camera, Writing Tools, and Smart Reply will also be available, as will audio transcription in Notes.

The Siri AI upgrade, which only occurred in other countries in 2026, won't be available at launch.

The current plan is for Apple to properly launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3's public release in December. With the news of registrations for iPadOS and macOS support in China, there's a good chance that the respective updates will also have Apple Intelligence at the same time.

items.title: How a Mac mini powers a staggeringly capable robot without human training
items.content_html:
Apple researchers have revealed how they use a Mac mini to control a Unitree humanoid robot to navigate rooms it has never seen before. It's really quite remarkable.

Leakers claiming that a future HomeView will have a robot arm didn't envisage anything like this. A team of researchers from Apple has published a paper detailing how they trained a Unitree G1 "humanoid" robot using an M4 Pro Mac mini with 64GB RAM.

Apple's "Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation" paper describes a system called "Humanoid Autonomy, Learned in Simulation, running Onboard," or HALO. The paper and its accompanying video show the Unitree G1 able to analyze rooms. It can follow someone if instructed, it can navigate obstacles, and when told to sit, determine where a chair is.

Apple is building humanoid robot brains.

This is a system that lets a Unitree G1 humanoid move around rooms it has never seen before. Tell it to "go sit on the chair," for instance, and it finds the chair, walks over and sits down. It can also crouch or crawl under tables, step through half-open doors and push boxes.

The robot carries an Apple Mac mini with an M4 Pro chip on its back. That computer runs the models that decide what to do and plan each movement. Nothing runs in the cloud, and nobody steers the robot remotely.

Most of the training data came from simulation: about 300 hours of humanlike movement, placed in 1,000 computer-generated living rooms, offices and bedrooms. Nobody teleoperated the robot to collect it.

The robot succeeded in 91% of 360 real-world trials across six skills.

All eight authors work at Apple, and the code is on GitHub.

— Humanoids daily (@humanoidsdaily) November 5, 2026

"Humanoid robots can somersault, dance, and run," says Apple in its paper. "Yet none of them can be invited into an unfamiliar living room and asked to sit down."

"They are agile but blind: a backflip is choreographed in advance and executed against geometry the robot never has to perceive," the researchers add.

Left: the prompts sent to the robot. Right: feeds from its cameras - image credit: Apple.

"The tasks that would make a humanoid useful are not like this," it continues. "They take place in rooms nobody has scanned, among furniture nobody has annotated, and the robot has to find the chair before it can sit on it."

What Apple did

The robot itself is from Unitree, not Apple, but the backpack it wears contains a high-spec M4 Pro Mac mini. The robot uses cameras to sense its surroundings, but then that data is compared to what it has already been trained on.

Apple's researchers trained the humanoid robot on around 300 hours of what they describe as synthetic data. Some 1,000 virtual rooms were generated and rendered in Nvidia's Isaac Sim.

Then when tested in the real-world, Apple says that its HALO system meant the humanoid robot completed 91% of 360 tasks. It did so across six environments that it had not seen before, and it did so without any operator controlling it.

Apple's testing involved six specific tests, such as telling it to crouch under a table, step through a half-open door, or sit on a chair. Each test was conducted 10 times in six real environments, and in 100 simulated rooms.

That 91% success rate is an average across both the real and virtual environments. In the real-world tests, it actually scored as high as 93% for the test of it stepping through a half-open door.

The poorest score it got in the real world was 85% success over sitting on a chair.

What Apple didn't do

Apple's researchers have laid out their work, including making the code available on GitHub, but they have also specified limitations in their testing. Perhaps the most significant is the robot's ability to perform any task still requires a human being to write the prompt.

So "the repertoire grows only as fast as a person can specify additional tasks." Then if those tasks were chained, so the robot was told multiple things to do in sequence, the success rate fell.

There is also the issue that none of the tests involved handling or manipulating objects.

What happens next

This isn't really going to be something seen in an Apple product soon. But that ability to perform these tasks using a Mac mini is remarkable to watch.

The research paper does not detail any future plans or objectives. However, it does say that the significance of its work here is that the robot was trained "by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data," rather than by human intervention.

"What would have taken hours (and days, and years) of human time can instead proceed autonomously and in parallel, bounded only by compute," says the paper.

items.title: iPhone Duo hinge issue down to bad parts, not bad design
items.content_html:
The spate of iPhone Duo screen issues has allegedly been traced to a material problem at a hinge component supplier, rather than there being a design flaw with the hinge itself.

Apple put a lot of work into designing the ideal hinge for the iPhone Duo, only to deal with reports of the hinge repeatedly failing in one specific place. It now seems that the problem was due to the components Apple used.

According to Chinese leaker Kang, reposted by Ice Universe, the hinge issues are due to the materials used for a specific component in the hinge. This is a component sourced from two suppliers.

A serial number can help Apple identify which units are affected by the bad components. However, it is unclear at this time if Apple will use it to recall devices, or if it will provide replacements.

An embarrassing problem

The discovery of component failure for an important mechanism in Apple's highest-profile device launch of the year is unfortunate. However, catching the issue early is helpful to Apple versus it surfacing later on, since it can fix the problem earlier.

Early teardowns of the iPhone Duo, as well as reports on social media, indicated that the screen would fail at the center crease of the hinge. Images showed that many of the claims appeared at the same general area of the display, pointing to some form of hinge problem.

https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/10/27/iphone-duo-hinge-maker-denies-blame-for-screen-failures

A closer examination by one YouTuber showed that one component had sheared completely, causing the damage. The component was a plate used to support the foldable OLED display during the folding and unfolding process.

The investigation showed there were heavy crush marks on a nearby mechanism that may have played a part in the breakage. An impact mark was also found under the display, possibly caused by the broken hinge element making contact.

The affair led to Apple hinge component supplier Fine M-Tec releasing a statement denying blame for the issue. It insisted that the damage wasn't caused by defects in its components, and that it would consider legal action against complaints without proper validation.

For its part, Apple acknowledged the social media reports on October 26, advising affected consumers to contact AppleCare for a replacement.

Probably still a small-scale issue

Social media reports and blog posts on those reports can make problems seem more widespread than they really are. As such, it's unclear exactly how many instances of this specific issue there are in the world.

That said, the problem is probably smaller than reports may indicate.

Example of how and where the iPhone Duo hinge is failing, breaking the screen

During the early stages of the issue, AppleInsider checked in with a number of U.S. Apple Store Genius Bars, including some major flagship locations. Initially, there didn't seem to be any reports, with that number growing to four after checking 20 stores by October 26.

Since that time, AppleInsider hasn't observed a significant increase in reports beyond low single digits.

So far, the affair seems to be in line with expectations of an initial device mortality rate at launch. Reports of broken devices shortly after the introduction of a new product is nothing new, and it doesn't seem as if this hinge issue goes far beyond that level.

items.title: iPad mini eighth generation review: Still the best e-reader, not an iPad Pro mini
items.content_html:
The OLED screen in the eighth generation iPad mini is a good reason to get the new model, but on the high end, for iPad Pro prices, it doesn't hit iPad Pro heights.

The iPad mini didn't start premium. At launch, it was a less expensive iPad, with a smaller form factor than the main line.

It's evolved into the pocket-sized powerhouse model, and it's had a pretty good existence so far. It is the best and most flexible e-reader anybody has ever made, for instance.

It's been two years since the last iPad mini update. And, in the midst of RAMpocalypse in 2026, the iPad 8 got a considerable upgrade beyond just that new OLED screen.

As always, the situation more complex than it looks on the surface.

iPad mini 8 review: A thinner, sealed design

At a glance externally, the iPad mini 8 is not redesigned, and retains the same design language as the last. It is a tiny bit thinner and lighter, though, so most of your old cases won't work.

iPad mini 8 review: The updated iPad mini 8 is significantly thinner, lighter, and a bit smaller than the outgoing model

It's still 7.69 inches long, but the width has been shaved from 5.3 inches to 5.22 inches.

More meaningfully different is the thickness, which has gone from 0.25 inches to 0.21 inches, or 0.63mm to 0.54mm. That's a 16% difference in thickness, which is massive even at this small scale.

iPad mini 8 review: The new speaker system is surprisingly effective

The speakers are different in the iPad mini this go-around. As such the unit gets an IP67 water rating. This does bring it in line with the iPhone lineup for water resistance, though you still wouldn't want to submerge or swim with it. More on that in a bit.

The color choice is also a little more basic in 2026. Gone are the colorful blue and purple, with your options now down to Starlight or Midnight.

It's not the end of the world, especially if you're the kind of person who invests in a case at the same time. And you're going to need a new one, since most don't fit.

If you haven't used the top-mounted iPad mini Touch ID before, that takes a bit of getting used to.

As it has always been, the build is solid.

iPad mini 8 review: The change to OLED

The OLED display is the main reason to care about the refresh. It is the non-Pro iPad's biggest upgrade in years, let alone the mini's.

The 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR panel replaces the backlit LCD. It's a hair larger than the previous model, thanks to the slimmer bezels.

iPad mini 8 review: The new OLED display with nanotexture

There's also a few more pixels to play with, at 2,316 by 1,512. It's still got the density of previous generations at 326 pixels per inch.

The hybrid OLED with LTPS panel gives it true blacks and per-pixel illumination control, which significantly helps the image quality. Colors are more vibrant, with the contrast ratio of 2 million to one helping it along the way.

It's also much brighter too, with it managing 600 nits for standard content. HDR pushes it further, with a peak of 1,200 nits.

This is a Pro-level display, with a big exception. The panel still runs at 60Hz, so you're not getting ProMotion here.

I don't think that Apple scored 60Hz OLED displays from the back of a truck somehow. As with much in 2026, this is about silicon.

It looks to me, based on some poking I've done, that the limit is in the controller chip. And based on that poking, it's about silicon availability and costs.

There is a giant price difference between a 60Hz controller and a 120Hz plus controller. Apple is fine with paying that on the iPad Pro, and on the Mac.

iPad mini 8 review: The new A20 Pro model (left) has slimmer bezels and more screen real estate than the old model (right)

It's apparently less fine on the iPad mini. I do expect it in an iteration or two down the road, but who knows how long that is going to take.

And yes, it does not matter as a media consumption tool. It absolutely does for gaming.

As such, there's a lot of screaming about this online. How much this matters very much depends on your own use case.

I'm glad my iPad Pro is ProMotion. I don't care that my iPad mini is not. Your mileage may vary, but to say that it doesn't matter that the iPad mini is 60Hz across the board is not a good take.

In daily use, you can tell if you put a ProMotion display next to this one. If that's aggravating depends user to user.

iPad mini 8 review: The nanotexture screen, combined with the brighter OLED display, make reading outside with the new iPad mini better than ever

You do still get the option to add a $100 Nano-texture glass treatment, so you can remove glare just like the premium models. You can't get this on the 128GB storage model to keep the number of SKUs down.

The display is a big change for the model and serves as an example of what to expect from Apple in the near future when it brings OLED to more products.

OLED on iPad mini for the first time, and Pulse Width Modulation

There is a lot to Pulse Width Modulation in electronics as a whole. As it pertains to the OLED display in iPad mini, Pulse Width Modulation is what Apple uses to regulate the brightness of individual color cells in the eye displays.

An incandescent bulb that can dim throws off fewer photons when at a lower wattage, roughly proportional to the magnitude of the cut in power. Provide half the power to an incandescent bulb, and it will be about half as bright. It does not turn off quickly and strobe — it just emits fewer photons because of the lower power.

In any OLED display, brightness control and color mixing is accomplished by turning individual color cells on and off very quickly. If full power, constantly, is being applied to a color cell, then that cell is "on time" or at a 100% duty cycle, and is fully bright.

Pulse width modulation and duty cycle example - credit circuitdigest.com

While there is an overall screen refresh frequency factor to consider as it pertains to health, in short, given a fixed frequency, to reduce the brightness, the color cell is extremely rapidly turned on and off.

This is complex, so we're going to simplify it a bit. A 50% duty cycle has the cell on or off half of the time, and is about half the brightness. It also effectively strobes the user at a different frequency than the display as a whole is doing.

Pulse Width Modulation has been used in OLED iPhones since the iPhone X, and it is important but not vital anymore to the operation of the screen. It has always been a health concern at some level, to some people.

If you haven't had sensitivity with your iPhone or iPad before, you're still good to go. But given that this is the first OLED iPad mini, it's worth talking about again.

Our advice is the same as it has always been. If you start feeling strange in any way while using iPad mini, or for that matter, anything with a screen, stop using it. Talk to your doctor about it.

And, there's Display Pulse Smoothing in accessibility on not just the iPhone, but this iPad mini too. It does impact low brightness performance, given that it is a reduction in voltage to cells, but that's a small price to pay if you're impacted by the strobing.

iPad mini 8 review: Camera and audio

While the display is the big change, the cameras are not. Changing the screen is certainly part of an enhanced spec-bump update, but not everything gets to change.

iPad mini 8 review: The new camera bump is smaller than before

The cameras carry over in spirit from the old model. The rear is a 12MP wide shooter at f/1.8, which is slightly disappointing.

It still records 4K video at up to 60fps, has a 5x digital zoom, and can use Smart HDR 4 for photographs.

The front is a little bit different. Sure, it's a 12MP Ultra Wide like before, but it's on the long edge for use in a landscape orientation. This is a change other iPad models have already undertaken, so it's nice to see here.

iPad mini 8 review: The front facing camera still lacks Face ID, but it has relocated to the landscape edge

The aperture is a little wider at f/2.0, and Center Stage is also in play for reframing your FaceTime calls.

For audio, there's a considerable difference. The landscape stereo speakers of the past are gone, in favor of a new Acoustic Display.

As the name implies the audio plays through the display, vibrating it. There's still has stereo audio support, which is nice.

That Acoustic Display is interesting. In short, the new speakers on the iPad mini shake the screen to help project the sound.

The sound is in fact richer than it is on the last few iPad mini models. It is not iPad Pro-level, nor even MacBook Pro level.

Apple is great at small-form speakers, but the physics of air movement are remorseless. I'm expecting this to come to the iPhone sooner rather than later, but the physics of the smaller screen may be limiting. We'll see.

There's no change to the microphones, though. There's still a pair of them used to capture your voice for calls.

They are fit for task, but you probably won't be recording your true crime podcast on them.

iPad mini 8 review: The A20 Pro and connectivity

Inside is Apple's A20 Pro chip. It is a three-generation jump over the old A17 Pro. That said, there's still a little variation depending on the model you get.

The 128GB and 256GB models use a 5-core CPU, with two super cores and three efficiency cores, as well as a 16-core Neural Engine.

iPad mini 8 review: The A20 Pro is powerful enough for excellent mobile gaming

If you splash out for the 512GB model, you get an extra efficiency core for the CPU, bringing the total to six cores. The Neural Engine is also upgraded to a Dual 16-core version, which will help with AI-centric tasks.

Both variants do benefit from a seven-core GPU with hardware-accelerated ray-tracing. More importantly, the per-GPU-core Neural Accelerators will further aid the Neural Engine with its tasks.

Apple is very much pushing AI as a big feature of its ecosystem. After the iPhones, it makes sense for the iPads to get the same treatment.

When it comes to benchmarks, the six-core variant achieves 3,945 in Geekbench 7 for the single-core test. The five-core version fares similarly, since the test deals with the single fastest available core, and that doesn't change.

Both are far ahead of the iPad mini 7, which achieves 2,526. The disparity is a sure sign of a multi-generational chip difference.

Moving to multi-core, the new iPad mini does differ, depending on the core counts. The higher-core version gets 11,192, with the lower hitting 9,837.

These are still miles better than the iPad mini 7's A17 Pro at 6,741.

On to Metal, and there's yet another massive difference in generations. The 20,526 of the iPad mini 7 is admirable, but the seven-core GPU in both A20 Pro variants destroys it at over 58,000.

Connectivity sees gains too. Wi-Fi moves to Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth to version 6. With the multi-year upgrade cycle for the iPad mini, this is a bit of future-proofing on Apple's side.

The USB-C port, primarily used for charging, stays at USB 3 and 10Gbps for data transfers. There is no Thunderbolt upgrade yet, but that is another thing you'd expect from a Pro model.

If you opt for a cellular model, you do get 5G connectivity once again. There is still no move on mmWave support though, so you're going to get sub-6GHz and that's it.

That is, unless you tether to an iPhone.

Battery life holds at the usual ten hours for video streaming, which isn't new for Apple. Ten hours is its general benchmark for the iPad mini battery.

What is interesting is that Apple does this with a slightly smaller cell.

The battery shrinks to 18.9 watt-hours, versus 19.3 watt-hours in the previous one. It's probably a combination of processing efficiency and the benefits of OLED at play, but it's a shame that it's not used for battery life to go up.

I'd have preferred that the iPad mini have stayed the same size as the previous model and eked out that 19.3 watt-hours.

iPad mini 8 review: More than a spec bump

The iPad mini 8 is a spec-bump update with one genuine exception in the form of the OLED display. It's one doozy of an exception.

iPad mini 8 review: The top has a power button with Face ID and the volume rockers

It's a change that gives the iPad mini a much more premium feeling. Before, it was a purposefully small tablet, but now it's one that you'd be more willing to show off.

There'll be no more feelings of inadequacy when it's placed next to an iPhone display. It's just as contrast-heavy and vibrant as your daily driver smartphone.

Pairing that with the A20 makes it a powerhouse without crossing the line into the realm of Pro.

What Apple has come up with is a pocket iPad Pro that's doesn't have as much multi-core grunt as the M-series chips, but still quite capable given that nearly every iPad mini use case is a single-core processing job.

The lack of LiDAR or ProMotion sets it apart from the Pro iPad line but the camera does the job in a pinch. Regardless, your iPhone camera, assuming it's newer than an iPhone 14 Pro, will be better than the cameras in even the iPad Pro.

At that launch I talked about earlier, the iPad mini was an option for users who wanted an iPad but without the size. Now, it's an option for someone who wants better than the baseline iPad, but also wants to avoid the sizing of the iPad Air.

The only real problem is the start price of $699 for 128GB of capacity. Sure, it's a jump up from the baseline iPad, but given the current state of the memory crisis and the chip and screen changes here, it's justifiable albeit unpleasant.

It's more unpleasant to pay $999 for the 512GB model and then another $100 for Nano-texture glass.

iPad mini 8 review: The new OLED display has amazing blacks and high contrast that looks fantastic on the small display

What Apple has managed to make is a compact tablet, that remains the best e-reader ever made, that doesn't have the bells and whistles of an iPad Pro. It's more portable than iPad Pro, it's just as fast for most tasks, and at the same time, the price hike makes me worry about how much that next iPad Pro is going to cost.

iPad mini 8 review - Pros

  • OLED display, a huge step up from LCD
  • Thinner, sealed body with IP67
  • Three-generation A20 Pro chip jump

iPad mini 8 review - Cons

  • Still 60Hz, with no ProMotion
  • $699 start, close to iPad Air money
  • Still no Face ID

Score: 4 out of 5

Scoring an entire line of iPads with a singular score for Google irks me, and it always has. There are clearly different markets for the low-end and high-end iPad mini.

There's already complaints about 128GB being too little for the iPad mini, but I disagree. At its core, the iPad mini is a consumption tool, and less of a content creator. The binned processor bears this out.

And at the higher-end, $999 is a lot to pay instead of going for an iPad Pro. At a thousand bucks it doesn't bring enough pro features for the price.

There's some discussion to be had about getting an iPhone 18 Pro, and an iPad mini with OLED screen instead of an iPhone Duo. The math falls apart on "cheaper" as you climb the scales on both units.

If you're in the market for both, you need to look at that cross-over very closely, and how you use both devices. In short, as always, it is down to individual workflow, the same as every other purchase decision.

For what it's worth, for as fun as the iPhone Duo is, I'm still on team "two separate devices."

We buy almost all of our review hardware. My 128GB purchased unit replaced my sixth generation iPad mini, and as you'd expect, it's better in every regard. It's expectedly faster in almost every task versus my 13-inch M1 iPad Pro. What the iPad mini is not, though, is a good Sidecar device, or particularly good for reading large format publications like technical manuals, comics or the rare magazine.

One of those tiny SSDs works great if I want to take along a massive amount of media, instead of accepting Apple's storage pricing.

I won't be returning it, and that is about the best praise that I can give new hardware.

Where to buy Apple's iPad mini 8

Apple's iPad mini 8 with an A20 Pro chip starts at $699, with Amazon, B&H, Expercom, and Adorama all carrying the compact tablet.

You can find the best iPad mini deals in our iPad mini 8 Price Guide.

items.title: Apple Stores ordered to stop signing up unwitting customers to services
items.content_html:
Staff at Apple Stores have been pressured into signing up customers to services such as Apple TV, but the practice has reportedly been stopped after it was uncovered.

Apple has previously cracked down on other firms pushing subscriptions on unwitting users, but now it has been doing something similar. Whether Apple expressly sanctioned it or just created the pressure on its employees, staff at Apple Stores have reportedly been signing up users to free trials without telling them.

The practice was uncovered by Louis Rossmann, previously best known as a critic of Apple's repair policies. In the latest of a series of YouTube videos, he has explained how the practice worked.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

When you go into an Apple Store and have your device set up, he says, staff can "also sign you up for subscriptions without your consent, because there is a screen that is on their device that has Accept or Decline." This is on their device, not the customer's, and so staff members have allegedly being pressing accept.

"They are encouraged to position subscriptions and free trials as gifts," continues Rossmann, "not telling the customer that 2 to 3 months from now, you are now going to have to pay $20 or $30 a month for whatever it is that they've signed you up for."

Apple stops the practice

Following Rossmann's initial YouTube video on October 30, 2026, he reports having had confirmation from Apple Store staff. According to one of these anonymous sources, though, Apple has abruptly banned the practice.

Reportedly, Apple has now issued an instruction to be "read verbatim in all stores" by regional managers. The text of that instruction hasn't been leaked yet, but this source claims it specifies that the "Accept" button must now only be pressed by the customer.

That source further says that the service metrics that staff work to have been changed. Specifically, Apple Stores allegedly no longer measure how many times each staff member has signed up a customer to a service.

It's obviously good if the practice has been disavowed. However, even if the source is accurate, it is not certain that this particular performance metric has been removed permanently.

Angela Ahrendts introduced the metrics when she took over Apple retail in 2013. At some point subsequently, Apple introduced a practice of stopping the metrics over the Christmas buying season.

When they are suspended like this, it's done in early November. It's not known when this first began, but it has happened before, and AppleInsider can confirm that these metrics have now been suspended for 2026.

So it may not be the case that this particular measure of staff performance is gone for good. But hopefully it does mean that this nickel-and-diming of Apple has been ended.

items.title: Sunday Reboot: Curses and a spotty reminder of times past
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, an exploration of Apple's expletives and transcriptions that are a step towards one 'Black Mirror' episode.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get next week underway with a good first step.

It isn't big, but it is clever

On Friday, a list of words and phrases that the iPhone simply won't recommend to you was published. Thousands of sentence fragments and words that can and will cause offense.

Words that Apple would shy away from suggesting as the next word in the sentence you're currently crafting.

Naturally, as someone who spends their life on the Internet, I just had to take a look. I'll gladly accept the accusations of being juvenile.

Since AppleInsider has standards to keep when it comes to writing about things, there's no way I can directly copy and paste a lot of what is on the list of suggestions. That's both for words and for the phrases.

I value being able to put my own words on this site too much to do that.

Expletives can be fun and sometimes educational.

Alas, as a British person who has seen too much Internet for one lifetime, I am not shocked by what appears on the lists. I had expectations of listings that I would be aware of but find mundane, and I was right.

I also had the expectation that there are phrases on the list that definitely deserve to be on there for painfully obvious reasons.

It was also educational, not only in the breadth of curses and vulgarities beyond my imagination, but also in how it is organized.

Let us take the two favorite "bombs" of the "F" and "C" variety.

Under the Full List for phrases, F-bombs appear in some form over 100 times on the list of phrases that won't be suggested. Under the Word Labels list, the term appears 93 times in total, including being inserted into a word as a tmesis.

By contrast, C-bombs are much fewer in number. In the single-word list, it only appears in five listings, and only three times in the phrases.

To me this is very surprising, as I can certainly come up with many more phrases using the term. I can come up with even more F-bomb phrases that were not included, but really should've been.

The way that Apple has managed to create the list is one that kinda avoids the so-called "Scunthorpe Problem." This refers to online systems blocking words in a filter because of a string or substring of letters that itself is blocked.

It looks as if Apple is preferring to define the offensive terms list by including variations, rather than taking out every instance of expletives that happen mid-word.

The method is far from all-encompassing, but at least it's being done in a smart way.

The potted history of me

The developer beta of iOS 27.3 brought with it a new Apple Intelligence feature, under its Audio Intelligence banner. Siri Recaps and Live Rewind were introduced during the September event as a way to help your everyday life, or at least to help you jog your memory via personal surveillance.

Using an Apple Watch Ultra 4 or Apple Watch Series 12, the wearables will listen to your conversations with other people. For privacy's sake, it will transcribe 15 second at a time, dumping the recording while saving the transcript for later, with the Secure Enclave also ignoring individual speakers identities.

The result is the creation of features like Live Rewind, which displays the last 15 seconds of transcribed text. Then there's Siri Recaps that will listen to an entire conversation and give you a summary of what was said.

As we discovered, it was pretty good at keeping track of what was said, albeit with some slight issues. In one imaged example, a conversation about housing were topped and tailed by details of a drunken fight and excitement for the reworking of a Zelda game.

A summary of a discussion, produced by Siri listening in.

The details are a little jarring but make sense considering the wider conversation, instead of a one-paragraph summary. If the main conversation was about one primary topic, side conversations about something completely unconnected only really warrants a mention and not a lot of detail.

It was also discovered that foul language wasn't included in Siri Recap, even if it was censored. Granted, it's not capturing quotes, so that sort of thing isn't needed.

The good thing about it is that it's not something that can really be used as a recording for legal purposes. It's hard to use an AI creating a summary from a transcript, itself based on a buffer that's living for 15 seconds at a time, as a serious form of evidence.

It's far from the everyman equivalent of police bodycams. At the same time, it's not that far off either.

Remember that Apple is in the process of creating smart glasses and AirPods with cameras, which could feasibly do the same thing, but with a view of the world. Again, Apple's need to conserve storage capacity and to enshrine privacy will mean it has a future for similar half-baked summaries of what happened.

It's not a world I particularly like the idea of living through. It seems like a few steps away from "The Entire History of You," an early episode from the dystopian sci-fi show "Black Mirror."

In the episode, society uses a "grain" to record what people see and hear, which can then be used to recall and rewatch memories.

I understand that it was written at a time when storage increases were expected to continue at a fast pace, enabling something like the grain McGuffin to exist at some point. So far, the AI industry is making that an impossibility.

In the show, the protagonist ends up down a rabbit hole thanks to the grain. He keeps rewatching his life and relationship, with the obsession wrecking his life in the process.

We are very far from that point, but even in the current simple form, it is something that could easily result in a similar scenario. Even though you're not getting all of the detail of a conversation, and with occasional slips and misheard elements, you're still getting enough to form an opinion after the fact.

It's already bad enough that the Internet never forgets. I wonder if we really need our iPhones to do the same.

Last week's Sunday Reboot discussed OpenAI's Sam Altman and his belief that memory is wasted in your Mac. It really should be part of the Great AI Globo-Industrial Machine.

items.title: Apple saves $2.7B in taxes by funnelling finances through Singapore
items.content_html:
Apple has saved $2.7 billion in taxes in 2026 thanks to funneling its finances through Singapore, better than its usual move involving Ireland.

As a massive multinational, Apple knows a thing or two about taxation and how to minimize its exposure to it. However, while Ireland has been seen as one of its main destinations to cut how much tax it pays, it did even better by using a different territory.

In an annual Apple disclosure in line with U.S. reporting rules, the Financial Times says Apple took advantage of the tax incentives in Singapore to a great effect. It funneled about $50 billion in profits through the Asian hub in 2026 alone.

The move helped cut $2.7 billion that would've been paid out in tax, and instead stays within Apple's accounts.

It turns out the savings are greater than what Apple saves from using its European HQ in Ireland. In the same timeframe, going through Ireland achieved a significant but slightly lower $2.6 billion tax saving.

Careful, Icarus

Apple does have a vested interest to try and spread its finances to other parts of the world, just to avoid paying too much tax.

The corporation taxes Apple paid totaled $27 billion this year. However, if it had been taxed on its global profits at the U.S. federal rate, the figure would've been $33 billion.

With such massive sums at play, Apple does have to try and be as tax-efficient as possible. Sometimes, this occurs to an extreme degree, and it has burned Apple before.

The biggest and most egregious example of tax saving is through Ireland, after the European Commission deemed Apple to have had illegal state aid. That was because Apple was charged just 0.005% tax in 2014 and 1% in 2003.

This resulted in a legal battle between Apple, Ireland, and the EU, as well as the payment of over $14 billion into an escrow account. Eventually, the European Court of Justice sided with the European Commission.

That resulted in Apple putting a $17 billion tax payment to Ireland in 2025, pushing the total up to $43 billion for the year.

items.title: Apple's iOS 28 schedule shift helps engineers get more creative
items.content_html:
Apple has experimented with how it develops its operating system updates, with early schedule changes in making the 28-gen updates, letting engineers become more creative earlier in the process.

Like any major project, Apple's annual operating system updates like iOS 27 require some intense scheduling. However, the way you schedule work can have a big impact on the final result.

According to Mark Gurman in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg on Sunday, Apple has made a tweak to how it works on its operating system updates.

For iOS 28 and iPadOS 28, known internally as Bell, as well as macOS 28, known as Poppy, the earliest stage of development was adjusted.

Apple has three major milestones for its operating systems, named M1, M2, and M3, throughout the annual cycle. The change occurred to M1, which has already passed.

Normally, each stage lasts for eight weeks, starting with four weeks of coding and then four weeks of convergence. The convergence refers to integrating the newly developed features into the operating systems.

However, this time around, Apple has shifted the split in favor of more coding in M1. That is, six weeks of coding and feature development followed by just two weeks of convergence.

A favorable shift

Employees apparently like this change, in part because it enables creativity. The engineers get more time to come up with ideas and to work through them, before having to lock them down and work them into the operating system.

This view certainly makes sense, especially if you consider the entire development cycle. As the year goes on, there will be a greater focus on correctly integrating the features into the operating system than earlier in the year.

Later stages will have previously added features from earlier stages to manage, as well as those incorporated in the milestone period. Earlier stages do not have this to worry about, so the convergence period isn't as important.

By shifting the schedule slightly, those early M1-stage features get more time to be worked on before convergence. The hope is that the extra time to come up with features will improve their overall quality too.

items.title: Siri AI won't get more control of Apple apps until Spring 2027
items.content_html:
Siri is already capable of handling some tasks for iOS 27.3 developer beta users. Apple is exploring making it even more useful to keep up with rival AI apps.

Developers in iOS 27.3 are discovering that Siri AI can do a lot more for users. For first-party apps, users can ask Siri what it can do, and then ask for it to carry out those same tasks.

However, this is only one step for Apple. It wants to do a lot more, both in terms of task complexity and for third-party apps too.

In Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman points out this Siri AI capability, but adds that this extended support for Apple's own apps can arrive to the public version in December.

Third-party support is still on the way, but that won't happen until the spring of 2027 as part of a "preview." This will probably be part of iOS 27.5 or iOS 27.6, ahead of the 2027 WWDC.

A more productive future

The moves, which Apple has planned as App Intents for quite some time, are important but behind other AI apps in terms of sophistication.

Services like Muse and Grok are capable of handling tasks and working between conversations. They can also elect to pause and resume work on their own, depending on the project's needs and the user's preferences over time.

Apple is allegedly trying to move in that direction, in terms of providing long-term assistance to users for specific tasks without necessarily needing user oversight every step of the way.

This more agentic style of Siri could also arrive early in 2027.

items.title: iPhone 18e will have the same larger battery as the iPhone 18
items.content_html:
A leaker with a mixed track record has released a diagram that purports to show the internal structures of the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, revealing that they have the same battery.

The most recent rumors about the iPhone 18 have claimed that it will have a larger battery, although it's possible this is just speculation. Now leaker Fixed Focus Digital has shown a diagram comparing the internal design of it to what is claimed to be the iPhone 18e.

While there are differences, such as with the cameras, a key part is a claim that the battery. The leaker emphasizes this, and also repeats a claim that many of the components of the two devices will be interchangeable.

There is a difference in the battery design, though, in that the diagrams list fractionally different capacities. "Taycan," a code for the iPhone 18 has its battery capacity listed as 3671 mAh to 4430 mAh.

In comparison, "Nevera," or iPhone 18e, has a battery with 4005 mAh to 4430 mAh.

The iPhone 18e may have the same battery as the iPhone 18 - image credit: Fixed Focus Digital.

That there is a range at all can be explained by how certain territories still require a physical SIM card. Other regions, including the US, can reclaim that space for a larger battery.

But the significant figure is probably the upper one, meaning that both phones will have a 4430 mAh battery. Given the leaker's claims and how the batteries appear in this purported diagram, the two phones do appear to use the same battery.

This backs up previous reports that claimed the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e would be more alike than different. They are expected to use the same processor, for instance, but they will have different cameras and displays.

Note that Fixed Focus Digital has only a mixed track record. Like most leakers on Weibo, they can just be echoing others, or simply speculating.

items.title: Apple leadership may have differing views on AI strategy
items.content_html:
A new report suggests Apple still faces internal battles around AI strategy even though it has seemingly held to the same strategy set by John Giannandrea nearly a decade prior.

The usual chatter and rumors that make it out of containment to reporters' ears suggest catastrophe and confusion within Apple even as evidence suggests otherwise. In a world where the AI bubble is bursting, if not at least deflating faster by the day, it's odd to see reports continue to suggest Apple has a poor strategy.

According to the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg, CEO John Ternus has asked Craig Federighi to produce more AI faster, even as the report contradicts itself and suggests Federighi's planning is already on too short of a timeframe. The report doesn't reflect the realities as they have been observed externally, where Apple has kept a cool head and avoided billions in losses and wasted investment versus its competitors.

There is no doubt some such meeting took place between Apple's software chief and CEO, but the tone of that meeting was likely very different. Those willing to share rumors based on "knowledge of the matter" likely have an axe to grind.

Then there's the added color and need for some kind of negative narrative from that publication. So, needless to say, this particular story can be taken with a grain of salt, just like with rumors of Srouji's departure.

The report goes on about other leadership position shifts and potential departures, but like we've learned, it's best not to dwell on such internal gossip and speculation until something happens.

Apple's AI strategy is well known

Apple hired John Giannandrea from Google in an effort to push its AI and ML strategy forward in 2018. His strategy focused on building powerful hardware that could handle smaller local models instead of chasing a trillion-dollar frontier model that required miles of data centers and GPUs.

In spite of suggestions otherwise, Apple has stuck to that strategy throughout. Investors did demand to see Apple's efforts in 2024, which led to an over-ambitious WWDC that promised more than Apple could deliver at the time.

A reset in approach, a rebuild of Siri, and a relaunch in 2026 with Google's Gemini frontier model at its core allowed Apple to maintain its focus in spite of mounting pressures. Today, Apple's hardware is among the best built for local AI processing. Its Apple Foundation Models serve good-enough private and secure functions useful for its user base.

Meanwhile, tech stocks drop as political pressure increases and the artificial demand represented by unfinished data centers is challenged by potential regulation. Apple remains unaffected by such moves and benefits from its private, secure, and local-first approach.
